analysis.one_liner: Caps Japanese car imports at roughly one in ten U.S. sales for three years.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote in the House Ways and Means Committee and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ordered the Commerce Secretary to hold Japanese car imports to 10.1 percent of total U.S. car sales in each of fiscal years 1993, 1994, and 1995, adjusting the cap each year based on the prior year's sales [S2] [S3]. That is an import quota: a hard ceiling on how many Japanese-made cars could enter the country. The idea was to shield American car makers and their workers from Japanese competition. The bill was introduced in late November 1991, referred to the Ways and Means Committee and its Trade Subcommittee, and never received any further action before the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: American-owned automakers and their employees would have gained the most: a smaller share of Japanese cars on the market means more American-made cars sold, protecting factory jobs and company profits. Some U.S. dealers of domestic brands and parts suppliers would also see more business.

how_it_helps.text: The bill caps Japanese vehicles at 10.1 percent of U.S. sales for fiscal years 1993 through 1995, calculated from the previous year's total sales, directly reducing the number of competing Japanese cars on the market [S3].

With fewer imports, demand shifts toward vehicles built by U.S. automakers, supporting American auto manufacturing employment — the stated rationale for trade-remedy bills like this one in the early 1990s [S2].

analysis.who_pays: American car buyers would have paid through higher prices and less choice. Quotas restrict supply, and when a popular product is capped, sellers can charge more. Shoppers who wanted specific Japanese models could have faced waiting lists, fewer options, or higher prices. Japanese automakers and their U.S. dealers and workers would also have lost sales.
analysis.who_pays_short: U.S. car buyers, in higher prices

drawbacks.text: A hard cap on imports means car buyers face higher prices and a smaller selection. When the government limits how many cars can be sold, the shortage is absorbed by consumers rather than by the companies, so the cost of protecting auto jobs is spread across everyone who buys a car [S3].

The quota could have invited retaliation from Japan against other U.S. exports, and it would have run against the general direction of U.S. trade policy at the time, which was moving toward lower trade barriers — reasons such bills typically die in the Ways and Means Committee without action [S1].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have protected a concentrated group — U.S. auto manufacturers and their workers — while spreading a real cost across every car-buying household. Historically, car import restrictions of this kind have raised prices for consumers by more than the wages saved, making this a poorly efficient bargain for the country as a whole, even though it would have delivered genuine, targeted help to a specific group of factory workers.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee and its Trade Subcommittee in November 1991, and nobody ever brought it up for a vote, so it simply expired when the two-year Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. John LaFalce, a New York Democrat, introduced the bill on November 26, 1991 [S1].
The same day, the House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee, which referred it further to its Subcommittee on Trade [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded; the bill's action history ends with the subcommittee referral [S5].
The bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, without ever reaching a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Japanese automakers and American car buyers came out ahead, since no quota was imposed and prices were never pushed up by an import cap. U.S. automakers seeking protection lost the opportunity, but they did not depend on this one bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Japanese automakers and U.S. car buyers

for.name: Rep. John J. LaFalce
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill capping Japanese car imports at 10.1 percent of U.S. sales for three fiscal years.

for.name: 9 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 10 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, referred it to the Trade Subcommittee, and never held a hearing or markup; the bill died there.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats (10 total), but no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of the full House is unknown; similar trade-protection bills generally drew mixed regional rather than strictly partisan support.

industries.note: The quota would have cut their U.S. sales to roughly a tenth of the market. Car buyers shared this interest, since less competition was expected to mean higher prices, so the industry's fate in this bill moved with consumers rather than against them.

Fewer Japanese cars on the market means more sales of American-built vehicles and protected factory output. Their gain would have come directly out of car buyers' pockets through higher prices and reduced choice.
Import limits were designed to preserve assembly and parts jobs in the U.S. auto sector. The cost of that protection would have been borne by consumers rather than by any single identifiable payer.
A cap on Japanese vehicles would shrink the inventory these dealers could sell. Their interest in blocking the quota ran alongside consumers', who faced the same loss of supply.
